docs.title: FaceTrack Developer Guide
docs.text:
Welcome to the official developer integration guide for FaceTrack by SOUL CAT Entertainment Sdn Bhd.

This documentation provides the technical specifications, file schemas, network protocols, and rigging kinematics required to integrate third-party applications, game engines, and virtual avatar runtimes.

Check out FaceTrack on Steam!

docs.title: System Overview & Architecture
docs.text:
FaceTrack uses NVIDIA RTX Maxine and Audio2Face deep-learning frameworks to extract high-fidelity facial performance metrics from webcam video, pre-recorded footage, or audio files.

The tracking system outputs a standardized 53-channel blendshape rig (based on the ARKit standard) paired with local head orientation quaternions. Facial tracking data is delivered through two distinct pipelines:

  • File Export Pipeline: Frame-by-frame baked data saved as either .ftd (a lightweight, sparse streaming log) or .json (human-readable structured data).
  • Live Capture Pipeline: Low-latency real-time UDP socket streaming transmitting head orientation and 53 blendshape coefficients simultaneously.

docs.title: Live Capture Integration Samples
docs.text: Here provide reference implementations for ingesting, parsing, and applying FaceTrack's real-time UDP stream across external toolsets and game engines. Whether you are building real-time telemetry visualizers in Python or driving digital human rigs inside Unity or Unreal Engine, these examples demonstrate reliable patterns for zero-latency socket handling and thread-safe data synchronization.

docs.title: Integration Architecture & Best Practices
docs.text:
• Thread Isolation: In game engines and UI frameworks, socket listening runs on a dedicated background thread to prevent UI freezing and avoid dropping UDP datagrams during heavy frame renders.
  • Range Normalization: FaceTrack outputs facial blendshape coefficients in a normalized 0.0 to 1.0 range. Runtimes requiring percentage-based inputs (such as Unity's SkinnedMeshRenderer, which expects 0 to 100) must scale the values accordingly.
  • Culture-Invariant Parsing: Floating-point numbers are transmitted with standard decimal points (.). Always parse using invariant culture (CultureInfo.InvariantCulture in C# or standard float() in Python) to prevent parse errors on systems configured with comma-based decimal locales.

docs.title: Python UDP Streaming Receiver
docs.text:
This lightweight script binds to port 9000, receives incoming datagrams, splits the orientation and blendshape segments, and extracts individual channel weights by index.

import socket

UDP_IP = "127.0.0.1"
UDP_PORT = 9000

# Initialize UDP socket
sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
sock.bind((UDP_IP, UDP_PORT))

print(f"FaceTrack UDP Receiver active on {UDP_IP}:{UDP_PORT}")

while True:
    data, addr = sock.recvfrom(2048)
    packet_str = data.decode("utf-8").strip()

    if "|" not in packet_str:
        continue

    rot_part, weights_part = packet_str.split("|", 1)

    # Parse Head Rotation Quaternion (qx, qy, qz, qw)
    qx, qy, qz, qw = [float(v) for v in rot_part.split(",")]

    # Parse 53 Blendshape Float Weights (0.0 to 1.0)
    blendshapes = [float(w) for w in weights_part.split(",")]

    # Access expressions by channel index
    jaw_open = blendshapes[26]
    blink_left = blendshapes[10]
    blink_right = blendshapes[11]

    print(f"JawOpen: {jaw_open:.2f} | Blinks: ({blink_left:.2f}, {blink_right:.2f})")

You can also download the full python receiver sample here to test out the Live Capture streaming.

docs.title: C# / Unity Receiver (Thread-Safe Runtime)
docs.text:
This component uses a background listener thread to prevent main-thread latency spikes in Unity. The incoming payload is locked, copied into thread-safe buffers, and applied to a SkinnedMeshRenderer during Unity's standard Update() loop.

using UnityEngine;
using System.Net;
using System.Net.Sockets;
using System.Text;
using System.Threading;
using System.Globalization;

public class FaceTrackLiveReceiver : MonoBehaviour
{
    [Header("Network")]
    public int listenPort = 9000;

    [Header("Target Mesh")]
    public SkinnedMeshRenderer faceMesh;

    [Header("Optional Head Transform")]
    public Transform headBone;

    private Thread receiveThread;
    private UdpClient udpClient;
    private bool isRunning = false;

    private readonly object lockObject = new object();
    private readonly float[] incomingBlendshapes = new float[53];
    private readonly float[] currentWeights = new float[53];
    private Quaternion incomingRotation = Quaternion.identity;
    private Quaternion currentRotation = Quaternion.identity;
    private bool hasNewFrame = false;

    void Start()
    {
        isRunning = true;
        receiveThread = new Thread(ReceiveThreadLoop) { IsBackground = true };
        receiveThread.Start();
    }

    private void ReceiveThreadLoop()
    {
        try
        {
            udpClient = new UdpClient(listenPort);
            IPEndPoint endPoint = new IPEndPoint(IPAddress.Any, listenPort);

            while (isRunning)
            {
                byte[] bytes = udpClient.Receive(ref endPoint);
                string message = Encoding.UTF8.GetString(bytes);

                int splitIndex = message.IndexOf('|');
                if (splitIndex < 0) continue;

                // 1. Parse Head Orientation Quaternion (qx, qy, qz, qw)
                string rotPart = message.Substring(0, splitIndex);
                string[] rotValues = rotPart.Split(',');
                Quaternion parsedRotation = Quaternion.identity;
                if (rotValues.Length == 4)
                {
                    float qx = float.Parse(rotValues[0], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
                    float qy = float.Parse(rotValues[1], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
                    float qz = float.Parse(rotValues[2], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
                    float qw = float.Parse(rotValues[3], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
                    parsedRotation = new Quaternion(qx, qy, qz, qw);
                }

                // 2. Parse the 53 comma-separated blendshape weights
                string weightsPart = message.Substring(splitIndex + 1);
                string[] bsValues = weightsPart.Split(',');

                if (bsValues.Length == 53)
                {
                    lock (lockObject)
                    {
                        for (int i = 0; i < 53; i++)
                        {
                            incomingBlendshapes[i] = float.Parse(bsValues[i], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
                        }
                        incomingRotation = parsedRotation;
                        hasNewFrame = true;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        catch (SocketException ex)
        {
            if (isRunning) Debug.LogWarning($"[FaceTrack] Socket exception: {ex.Message}");
        }
    }

    void Update()
    {
        lock (lockObject)
        {
            if (!hasNewFrame) return;

            System.Array.Copy(incomingBlendshapes, currentWeights, 53);
            currentRotation = incomingRotation;
            hasNewFrame = false;
        }

        // Apply head rotation if bound
        if (headBone != null)
        {
            headBone.localRotation = currentRotation;
        }

        // Apply weights (FaceTrack outputs 0.0–1.0; Unity blendshapes require 0–100)
        if (faceMesh != null && faceMesh.sharedMesh != null)
        {
            int shapeCount = Mathf.Min(53, faceMesh.sharedMesh.blendShapeCount);
            for (int i = 0; i < shapeCount; i++)
            {
                faceMesh.SetBlendShapeWeight(i, currentWeights[i] * 100.0f);
            }
        }
    }

    void OnDestroy()
    {
        isRunning = false;
        udpClient?.Close();
        receiveThread?.Abort();
    }
}

docs.title: File Export Pipeline
docs.text:
The File Export Pipeline allows animators, technical artists, and developers to extract recorded facial performance capture data from FaceTrack for offline processing, editing, and integration into standard 3D animation workflows.

By decoupling the capture session from runtime rendering, you can cleanly import raw performance data into your Digital Content Creation (DCC) application of choice—such as Blender, Maya, Unreal Engine, or Unity—to refine keyframes, retarget morph targets, and layer secondary animation.

docs.title: Key Capabilities
docs.text:
• Full Fidelity Capture: Exports frame-accurate facial blendshape coefficients and 6-DOF head kinematics.
  • Flexible Tooling Support: Choose between streamlined binary storage or accessible structured text depending on pipeline requirements.
  • Non-Destructive Integration: Import tracked data as layered animation clips or modifier curves without altering base rig hierarchies.

docs.title: Supported Export Formats
docs.text: Format Extension Primary Use Case Characteristics FaceTrack Data .FTD Production DCC animation, DCC importer add-ons Compact binary structure, optimized for performance and minimal file size. JSON .JSON Pipeline scripting, engine tools, custom parsers Human-readable, schema-driven, and easy to parse across any programming language.

docs.title: Blender Add-on
docs.text:
You can download the official importer add-on for Blender here.

  • Supported Versions: Blender 5.2+
  • Features: Automatic rig detection, shape key curve generation, and framerate synchronization.

docs.title: FaceTrack Data File (.FTD)
docs.text: The .ftd format is a lightweight plaintext data format optimized for continuous capture storage without timestamp overhead.

docs.title: Frame Structure
docs.text:
1. Head Orientation Line: 4 comma-separated floating-point values representing quaternion axes: qx,qy,qz,qw.

  2. Blendshape Channel Lines: Sparse key-value pairs formatted as <channel_index> <weight>.

  3. Channels with values \(\le 0.0001\) are omitted to reduce file size.

  4. Weights are normalized floats between 0.0 and 1.0.

  5. Frame Delimiter: A single right-angle bracket > on its own line signals the end of the current frame.

docs.title: FaceTrack JSON File (.JSON)
docs.text: The .json file contains structured, pretty-printed frames intended for non-realtime DCC authoring and manual animation cleanup.

docs.title: Frame Structure
docs.text:
The root JSON object encapsulates global capture metadata and an array of sequential frame data:

  1. Global Properties:
  2. targetFPS: An integer designating the capture and authoring framerate (e.g., 30, 60).

  3. frames: An array containing sequential frame objects in chronological capture order.

  4. Frame Object Properties (frames[]):

  5. headRotation Object: Local-space rotation quaternion defined across four floating-point properties:
    • x: Float representing the \(q_x\) axis component.
    • y: Float representing the \(q_y\) axis component.
    • z: Float representing the \(q_z\) axis component.
    • w: Float representing the \(q_w\) scalar component.
  6. blendshapes Array: An ordered list of expression objects defining facial weights:
    • name: String identifier corresponding to the FaceTrack 53-channel blendshape standard (e.g., "browDownLeft").
    • value: Normalized floating-point weight between 0.0 and 1.0.

docs.title: Live Capture Pipeline
docs.text:
The Live Capture Pipeline enables real-time, low-latency streaming of facial performance capture and head pose kinematics directly over a local network. Built for interactive use cases—including virtual production in Unreal Engine or Unity, live VTubing, and real-time avatar puppeteering—it delivers frame-by-frame tracking data synchronously without the overhead of heavy transport protocols.

By broadcasting lightweight UDP datagrams, FaceTrack allows any external software or custom runtime client to ingest facial animation coefficients with minimal latency and zero handshaking overhead.

docs.title: Key Capabilities
docs.text:
• Minimal Transport Latency: Uses connectionless UDP sockets to avoid head-of-line blocking and eliminate packet retransmission lag.
  • Unified State Transmission: Delivers normalized 6-DOF head orientation and all 53 facial blendshape channels synchronized in a single packet.
  • Flexible Deployment: Supports single-machine loopback pipelines (127.0.0.1) as well as dedicated multi-machine LAN broadcast configurations.
  • Engine-Agnostic Ingestion: Compatible with any programming environment supporting standard socket programming (C#, C++, Python, Rust).

docs.title: Configuration & Activation
docs.text:
To start streaming tracking data from FaceTrack:

  1. Navigate to Settings > Live Capture.
  2. Toggle Enable Streaming on.
  3. Switch FaceTrack to Avatar Preview mode.

Status Indicator: Data is transmitted only while in Avatar Preview mode. A chain icon appears in the interface to indicate an active broadcast state.

docs.title: Default Socket Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Value Notes Protocol UDP (User Datagram Protocol) Fast, connectionless transport. Default Host / IP 127.0.0.1 Local loopback (same-machine streaming). Default Target Port 9000 Configurable receiving port.

docs.title: Local Network (LAN) Setup
docs.text:
To stream data from FaceTrack to another computer across a local network:

  1. In FaceTrack settings, set the bind address / IP to 0.0.0.0 (listens on all available network interfaces).
  2. On the receiving machine (e.g., a secondary workstation running Unreal Engine), configure the client listener to target the local IPv4 address of the host machine running FaceTrack (e.g., 192.168.1.X).
  3. Firewall Requirements: Ensure inbound UDP traffic on port 9000 is permitted on the host machine. You may need administrative privileges to create an inbound firewall rule in Windows Defender or corporate firewall tools.

docs.title: Datagram Payload Format
docs.text:
Each packet is serialized as a raw, human-readable UTF-8 string divided into two distinct sections by a vertical bar delimiter (|):

<qx>,<qy>,<qz>,<qw>|<val_0>,<val_1>,<val_2>,...,<val_52>

docs.title: Blendshapes Implementation
docs.text: FaceTrack outputs 53 facial blendshape channels (indexed 0 to 52) based on the ARKit standard for easy integration with existing DCC applications.

docs.title: 53 Facial Blendshape Channels
docs.text:
Here are the 53 blendshapes channels, with both browInnerUp and cheekPuff split into bilateral (Left/Right) targets:

Index Blendshape Name Category 0 browDownLeft Eyebrows 1 browDownRight Eyebrows 2 browInnerUpLeft Eyebrows 3 browInnerUpRight Eyebrows 4 browOuterUpLeft Eyebrows 5 browOuterUpRight Eyebrows 6 cheekPuffLeft Cheeks 7 cheekPuffRight Cheeks 8 cheekSquintLeft Cheeks 9 cheekSquintRight Cheeks 10 eyeBlinkLeft Eyes 11 eyeBlinkRight Eyes 12 eyeLookDownLeft Eyes 13 eyeLookDownRight Eyes 14 eyeLookInLeft Eyes 15 eyeLookInRight Eyes 16 eyeLookOutLeft Eyes 17 eyeLookOutRight Eyes 18 eyeLookUpLeft Eyes 19 eyeLookUpRight Eyes 20 eyeSquintLeft Eyes 21 eyeSquintRight Eyes 22 eyeWideLeft Eyes 23 eyeWideRight Eyes 24 jawForward Jaw 25 jawLeft Jaw 26 jawOpen Jaw 27 jawRight Jaw 28 mouthClose Mouth 29 mouthDimpleLeft Mouth 30 mouthDimpleRight Mouth 31 mouthFrownLeft Mouth 32 mouthFrownRight Mouth 33 mouthFunnel Mouth 34 mouthLeft Mouth 35 mouthLowerDownLeft Mouth 36 mouthLowerDownRight Mouth 37 mouthPressLeft Mouth 38 mouthPressRight Mouth 39 mouthPucker Mouth 40 mouthRight Mouth 41 mouthRollLower Mouth 42 mouthRollUpper Mouth 43 mouthShrugLower Mouth 44 mouthShrugUpper Mouth 45 mouthSmileLeft Mouth 46 mouthSmileRight Mouth 47 mouthStretchLeft Mouth 48 mouthStretchRight Mouth 49 mouthUpperUpLeft Mouth 50 mouthUpperUpRight Mouth 51 noseSneerLeft Nose 52 noseSneerRight Nose

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text: Keep in mind that cheekPuffLeft, cheekPuffRight are always set to zero as they are currently not supported. Tongue blendshapes are also omitted due to technical limitation.

docs.title: Rigging & Kinematics Implementation
docs.text: Target rigs can receive tracking either through direct mesh morphs (Blendshapes / Shape Keys) or bone rotations.

docs.title: Head Rotation & Fallback Morphs
docs.text:
The raw rotation quaternion arrives in \([q_x, q_y, q_z, q_w]\) ordering.

  • Blender Conversion: Reorder components to scalar-first: \((q_w, q_x, q_y, q_z)\).

  • Unity Conversion: Negate \(y\) and \(z\) axes for left-handed coordinate systems: new Quaternion(qx, -qy, -qz, qw).

When rigging characters without head bone hierarchies, calculate equivalent head morphs using Euler bounds:

  • Range limits: \(\text{Turn Up/Down} \in [-45^{\circ}, 45^{\circ}]\), \(\text{Turn L/R} \in [-76.5^{\circ}, 76.5^{\circ}]\), \(\text{Tilt L/R} \in [-35.1^{\circ}, 35.1^{\circ}]\).

  • Linear remap formula:

\[\text{Value} = \left(\frac{\theta - \theta_{\min}}{\theta_{\max} - \theta_{\min}}\right) \cdot 3.0 - 1.5\]

docs.title: Eye Gaze Kinematics
docs.text:
Eye look channels (indices 12 to 19) can actuate bone rotations (Pitch and Yaw) using the differential weights between opposing directions:

\[\text{Pitch}_{\text{Left}} = (w_{18} - w_{12}) \cdot \theta_{\text{pitch\_max}} \cdot s_{\text{vert}}\] \[\text{Yaw}_{\text{Left}} = (w_{14} - w_{16}) \cdot \theta_{\text{yaw\_max}} \cdot s_{\text{horiz}}\] \[\text{Pitch}_{\text{Right}} = (w_{19} - w_{13}) \cdot \theta_{\text{pitch\_max}} \cdot s_{\text{vert}}\] \[\text{Yaw}_{\text{Right}} = (w_{17} - w_{15}) \cdot \theta_{\text{yaw\_max}} \cdot s_{\text{horiz}}\]

  • Default Angular Bounds: Pitch Range = \(15.0^{\circ}\), Yaw Range = \(25.0^{\circ}\) (or \(45.0^{\circ}\) depending on rig sensitivity).

  • Horizontal/Vertical sign scalars: \(s_{\text{horiz}} = -1.0\) (when horizontal flip is enabled), \(s_{\text{vert}} = 1.0\).
